name: view-handler
intent: Give one component the ownership of a model's views - creating, opening, switching, disposing and notifying them - so that views never manage each other and clients never hold view objects directly.
problem: A model is presented through several views at once (several documents open, or one document shown as table, chart and form), and each view is created, closed and refreshed on its own: view lifecycle code is duplicated, meta-operations that need the whole set (tile, cascade, arrange, close-all) have no owner, and every model ends up implementing its own publisher registry just to tell its views that something changed. The recurring trigger is that one object must own creating, switching and syncing a model's several views.
context: Presentation layers with long-lived views over a shared model: multi-document editors and IDEs, diagram/CAD tools with several viewports, dashboards where one dataset is shown as chart, table and summary, plugin hosts where view types arrive at runtime, and web or mobile shells that mount one screen at a time out of several registered views. It applies when several views must live at once or be switched dynamically, when view meta-operations act on the set rather than on a single view, and when models should not each carry an observer registry of their own.
benefits: One owner for view lifecycle: creation, opening, switching, disposal and the meta-commands that act on all views (tile, cascade, arrange, close-all) are implemented once instead of being distributed across views, documents and controllers.
Clients address views by a handle or a type instead of an object reference, so a caller cannot keep a disposed view alive by accident and the handler can enforce that only it creates views.
New view types plug in through the handler's factory or type registry, so adding a chart, an outline or a third-party view leaves the existing views untouched.

Models stop being publishers: a model signals the handler once and the handler fans the change out to the views that show it, replacing one observer registry per model with a single coordination point.
Views stay independent of each other - they do not know their siblings - while dependencies such as 'refresh the outline when the table selection moves' are expressed in the handler.
Uniform handling gives users consistency: every view opens, closes, activates and refreshes the same way because uniformity is imposed by one component instead of being negotiated by each view.
tradeoffs: The handler is a coupling hub: views hold a reference to it and, in the classic singleton form, so does the model, which pulls presentation infrastructure into the domain layer and makes tests depend on global state.

Change propagation is coarse: notifying every open view on every model change costs work proportional to the number of open views and re-renders views that were not affected, unless dependencies are tracked or redraws are coalesced.

The registry is a lifetime hazard: a view that is closed but not removed is leaked and keeps receiving notifications, while a handle kept past disposal becomes a dangling reference - creation and disposal therefore have to be a matched pair.
Notification re-entrancy: a view that opens, closes or activates another view inside its update mutates the registry while the handler iterates it.

Uniformity has a price: views must share an interface or be adapted, so unmodified third-party widgets cannot participate, and the handler tends to accumulate view-specific decisions that belong in the views.

Modern UI frameworks already provide the role (MDI areas, window/route/screen containers, navigation controllers), so hand-building the structure on top duplicates framework machinery and fights its lifecycle.

participants.responsibility: Owns the set of views: keeps the registry of open views with their identities, creates and disposes views through its factory, implements the view meta-commands, and propagates model changes to the views that are affected.

A presentation object with a uniform interface (show/update, activate/deactivate, close) that obtains its data from the model; it registers with the handler rather than with its sibling views, and only the handler creates it.

The data and behaviour being presented; when its state changes it asks the view handler to propagate the change, so in the classic form the model holds a reference to the handler instead of maintaining observers of its own.
Issues view commands - open a view of this type, switch to it, close it, tile the open views - normally with a handle returned by the handler, and turns user input into model or view requests.

The creation mechanism inside the handler: a table of prototypes or constructors keyed by view type from which a new view instance is cloned or instantiated; a separate collaborator when view types are contributed by plugins.

use_cases: Multi-document editors and IDEs: one document opened in several windows (clone window) plus outline, properties and console panels that must be tiled, cascaded and closed together when the application quits.
Analytics and reporting tools where one dataset is shown simultaneously as table, chart and summary, and a selection in one view must be reflected in the others.
Diagram, CAD and simulation tools with several viewports (overview, zoomed detail, layer list) bound to a single scene.
Plugin hosts and extensible shells where view types arrive from plugins and are instantiated by type name through the handler's factory instead of being wired statically.
Mobile or desktop shells with a registry of screens or tabs (navigation controller, tab host, stacked pages) that switch the active view while the others keep their state.
Presentation-independent renderers: one report model rendered to HTML, PDF and CSV views that a coordinator creates in order and keeps consistent.

Win32 MDI: the operating system ships the handler as a preregistered MDICLIENT window - applications send WM_MDICREATE, WM_MDIACTIVATE and WM_MDIDESTROY to it for lifecycle and WM_MDITILE, WM_MDICASCADE and WM_MDIICONARRANGE as set-wide meta-commands, routing through DefFrameProc instead of owning a view registry themselves.

Qt widgets: QMdiArea is a ready-made view handler - addSubWindow/removeSubWindow are the matched create/dispose pair, subWindowList()/activeSubWindow() the registry, closeAllSubWindows() the close-all command and cascadeSubWindows()/tileSubWindows() the layout meta-operations, so MDI applications configure the handler instead of writing one.

Java Swing: JDesktopPane hosts JInternalFrame views and delegates the window-management behaviour to a pluggable DesktopManager supplied by the look-and-feel - an injected view handler, showing the pattern working without a global singleton.
avoid_when: The model has exactly one view: a direct update call or the framework's own observer mechanism is simpler than a registry of one.

The UI framework already owns view lifecycle and switching (Qt MDI or stacked widgets, WPF windows, UIKit or AndroidX navigation controllers, a browser router) - configure it instead of rebuilding the roles.
Views are stateless render functions of application state (immediate-mode and declarative toolkits): there are no retained view objects to own, so derive the UI from state and drop the handler.
Views are produced per request on a server (template view or composite view pages): nothing lives long enough to be registered.
The set of views is fixed and small (a two-pane form): wiring both views to the model directly is clearer than a general registry with handles and commands.
anti_patterns: "God window manager": the handler also implements view-specific rendering and business decisions, so views degrade into data bags and the coordinator becomes the hardest class to change.
Ambient singleton handler reachable from everywhere, including the model, so the domain layer depends on presentation infrastructure and every test needs the global to exist.
Notify-everything synchronisation presented as consistency: each model mutation wakes every open view, unrelated views repaint, and re-entrancy bugs surface as flicker or runaway update loops.
A registry of handles that outlive their views - closing a window removes it visually but leaves the entry, so the handler keeps disposing and notifying ghosts.
Rebuilding the roles on top of a framework that already provides them (MDI areas, navigation controllers, routers), producing two competing view registries that drift apart.
Shared view instances across documents with per-document state smuggled in through globals.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: managing views is a different responsibility from presenting data or handling input, so it belongs to a component of its own.
Single ownership: exactly one component creates, registers and disposes views, which turns view lifetime into a closed bookkeeping problem.
Information hiding: clients and models address views through handles and commands, never through view internals.
Open/closed: new view types enter through the factory or registry without edits to the handler or to the existing views.
Don't repeat yourself: view meta-operations over the whole set (layout, close-all, refresh) are written once.
Explicit lifetime: every registration has a matching disposal.
best_practices: Make the handler the only creator: views are instantiated through its factory or type registry, which lets it register a view before anyone else can obtain it.
Return a handle from open() and require it for every later operation, with a defined failure mode for unknown or already-closed handles.
Treat close as remove-then-dispose and keep registration and disposal symmetric, so no path leaks a view.
Collect the notification targets before calling into views, so a view that opens or closes another view cannot corrupt the iteration.
Track or declare which part of the model each view observes, and coalesce refreshes per frame or tick instead of redrawing every view on every change.
Keep the handler free of view-specific logic: give each view type a uniform interface or adapter rather than letting the coordinator make rendering decisions.
When the platform already supplies the registry (MDI area, navigation controller, router, fragment manager), delegate to it and keep only the policy the platform does not know about.
Keep the model's link to the handler explicit and injected rather than global, so domain tests run without a UI.
